intro:
Al-Fātiḥah is the chapter that opens the Book. Its name means "The Opening", and it carries that name for two reasons: the Book of Allah begins with it, and every unit of prayer begins with it as well. No prayer is complete without it, which is why the scholars call it the key to the whole Qur'an.

Most of the early authorities place its revelation in Makkah. Ibn Kathīr records that Ibn ʿAbbās, Qatādah and Abū al-ʿĀliyah all held that view, and the majority of the scholars followed them. Al-Alūsī preserves the one voice on the other side: Mujāhid said it came down in Madinah, and the scholars who came after him counted that as a slip. The practical argument settles the question. The five prayers were made obligatory in Makkah, and the prayer is not valid without this chapter. The Muslims must therefore have had it in their hands before they left Makkah. Al-Suyūṭī collects the reports on both sides in one place. ʿAlī is recorded by al-Wāḥidī and al-Thaʿlabī as saying that the chapter came down in Makkah from a treasure beneath the Throne. Against that, Ibn Abī Shaybah and Abū Nuʿaym report Abū Hurayrah saying that Iblīs wailed when the chapter was revealed, and that its revelation came in Madinah. The weight of the evidence still leans to Makkah, and the majority of the commentators say so.

The chapter has several names, and each one describes a different job it does. Ibn Kathīr lists them from the early reports. It is al-Fātiḥah, the Opener. It is Umm al-Kitāb and Umm al-Qurʾān, the Mother of the Book and the Mother of the Qur'an, because everything in the Book is gathered in it. Ibn Sīrīn disliked that second name, and al-Suyūṭī records his reason: the Qur'an uses the phrase for Allah's own record, in the verse (13:39 — **“Allah eliminates and confirms what He wills, and with Him is the Master Record”**), so he preferred to say Fātiḥat al-Kitāb. It is al-Sabʿ al-Mathānī, the Seven Oft-Repeated Verses, a name the Qur'an gives it directly: (15:87 — **“We have certainly granted you the seven often-repeated verses and the great Quran”**). It is also called al-Ḥamd and al-Ṣalāh, because it is praise from beginning to end and because the prayer is named after it. Two more names describe what it does for a reader: al-Shifāʾ, the Cure, and al-Ruqyah, the healing recitation.

The scholars counted its letters with care. Ibn Kathīr reports that the chapter holds twenty-five words and one hundred and thirteen letters. Al-Qurṭubī gave it twenty-seven separate questions in his commentary, because so many rulings and meanings sit inside those few lines. Al-Bukhārī explained the mother-name in the simplest way: the Qur'an starts with it, and the prayer starts by reciting it. Ibn Jarīr al-Ṭabarī added the Arabic behind the name. The Arabs call any matter that gathers many parts an umm. They call the skin around the brain umm ar-raʾs, and the banner that gathers the army an umm, and Makkah Umm al-Qurā because it leads the settlements.

Its rank in the Book is described in the hadith. At-Tirmidhī, who graded the report ṣaḥīḥ, records Abū Hurayrah hearing the Prophet ﷺ call it the Mother of the Qur'an, the Mother of the Book, the seven repeated verses and the glorious Qur'an. Aḥmad records Abū Saʿīd ibn al-Muʿallā being told that he would be taught the greatest sūrah in the Qur'an, and discovering that it was this one. Aḥmad also records Ubayy ibn Kaʿb being told that nothing like it had been sent down in the Torah, the Gospel, the Psalms or the Qur'an; At-Tirmidhī received the same report and graded it ḥasan ṣaḥīḥ. Muslim and An-Nasāʾī record Ibn ʿAbbās describing a door in heaven opened for this Prophet ﷺ alone, from which an angel brought two lights no prophet had been given before: the Opening of the Book and the closing verses of Sūrah al-Baqarah. Its use as a healing recitation is in the two Ṣaḥīḥs, where Abū Saʿīd al-Khudrī treated a stung tribal chief with it, and the Prophet ﷺ asked him how he knew it was a healing recitation, then told the group to divide the sheep they had been paid and give him a share.

Two rulings keep the chapter in a Muslim's life every day. Muslim records Abū Hurayrah reporting that the Prophet ﷺ said three times that whoever prays without Umm al-Qur'an has prayed incompletely. When Abū Hurayrah was asked what a person standing behind the imam should do, he answered that such a person should recite it quietly, and he quoted the ḥadīth qudsī behind the ruling: "I have divided the prayer between Myself and My servant into two halves, and My servant shall have what he asks for." The two Ṣaḥīḥs record ʿUbādah ibn al-Ṣāmit reporting the same requirement in a harder form, "There is no prayer for whoever does not recite the Opening of the Book."

The chapter has one clear turn. Verses 1:1 to 1:4 speak about God: His Name, His praise, His mercy, His mastery of the Day of Judgement. Verse 1:5 turns and speaks to Him. The last two verses are requests that God Himself taught the servant to make. Maʿārif al-Qurʾān notes that the middle verse holds both halves at once, because "You alone we worship" is praise and "You alone we ask for help" is a request. The ḥadīth qudsī in Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim describes the chapter as divided into two halves between Allah and His servant, and the dividing line falls exactly at that verse. The whole chapter is spoken in the plural, so the one praying speaks for every believer. Maudūdī's Tazkir al-Qurʾān sums it up: this chapter is Islam in miniature, and the rest of the Qur'an is the enlargement of that picture.

One story shows what the chapter does to a heart that meets it for the first time. Al-Suyūṭī records, through a man of the Banū Salimah, that when the tribe accepted Islam, the wife of the elderly ʿAmr ibn al-Jamūḥ urged her husband to listen to what his son had learned. The son recited the chapter to him. The old man, who had spent his life outside this message, listened to the end and said: how beautiful and how fine this is; is all of it like this? The report is soft in its chain, and it is recorded as a story rather than a proof. Its point is still worth holding. A page of the Qur'an, read plainly to a person who has never heard it, can carry its own weight.

verses.1:
> In the Name of Allah—the Most Compassionate, Most Merciful

**THE LINE THAT OPENS THE BOOK**

This line is called the basmalah. It stands at the head of one hundred and thirteen chapters of the Qur'an. Only Sūrah al-Tawbah opens without it. Inside the text of the Qur'an it appears one other time, in the letter the Prophet Sulaymān sent to the Queen of Sheba: (27:30 — **“It is from Solomon, and it reads: ‘In the Name of Allah—the Most Compassionate, Most Merciful”**).

The first word of revelation ever brought to the Prophet ﷺ carried the same instruction: (96:1 — **“Read, ˹O Prophet,˺ in the Name of your Lord”**). The Muslim begins with the Name of Allah because the Qur'an begins there, and because God is the one who makes every act possible. Al-Ṭabarī opens his commentary on the line with a reason drawn from God's own teaching. Allah trained His Prophet ﷺ to place His Name in front of every action, and then made that habit a duty for the whole community. The word for the opening phrase, ***“In the Name of Allah”***, teaches the servant where the power for the work ahead actually comes from. He does not begin with his own strength and finish with a report of his own success.

**IS THE BASMALAH A VERSE OF THIS CHAPTER?**

Whether the line is a verse of this chapter became a long discussion among the early Muslims, and al-Suyūṭī gathers the reports. Ibn Sīrīn reports that Ubayy ibn Kaʿb wrote it at the head of his copy of the Book, that ʿUthmān ibn ʿAffān wrote it, and that Ibn Masʿūd did not write it at all. The man himself is recorded as saying that if he were to write it, he would have to write it at the head of everything. Al-Dāraquṭnī records Abū Hurayrah reporting, in a chain he graded sound, that the Prophet ﷺ said: when you recite al-Ḥamd, recite the basmalah, for it is the Mother of the Qur'an, the Mother of the Book, the seven repeated verses, and one of its verses. Umm Salamah is recorded as saying that the Prophet ﷺ recited it as part of the chapter, and he told her the chapter was seven verses with it. Different copies, and different practice, but the words themselves are agreed by everyone.

**NAMES THE EARLY COMMUNITY GAVE THE LINE**

The early Muslims also gave the line names of its own. Sufyān ibn ʿUyaynah called it al-Wāfiyah, the Complete. ʿAbd Allāh ibn Yaḥyā ibn Abī Kathīr called it al-Kāfiyah, the Sufficient, and explained the name in a way that stays in the mind: it stands in for other words, and nothing else stands in for it. Al-Shaʿbī, when a man complained to him of a pain in his side, told him to hold on to the foundation of the Qur'an, and that is what he called this line. A report from Ibn ʿAbbās, carried by al-Khaṭīb al-Baghdādī in weak chains, calls it the key of every book. A key is a small thing to hold and it opens everything behind it.

**WHY IT WAS SOMETIMES SAID ALOUD**

Al-Suyūṭī also shows why the words were sometimes spoken aloud and sometimes not. Saʿīd ibn Jubayr reports that the Prophet ﷺ used to raise his voice with the basmalah in Makkah, until the people of Quraysh, who had given the name al-Raḥmān to the false prophet Musaylimah, began to say that Muhammad was calling on the god of Yamāmah. God then instructed His Prophet ﷺ to lower his voice with it, and he kept it quiet until he passed away. Ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn Mughaffal reports the practice of the men around him: he said, my son, that is an innovation; I prayed behind the Prophet ﷺ, behind Abū Bakr, behind ʿUmar and behind ʿUthmān, and none of them recited it aloud. Ibn Mājah and the two Ṣaḥīḥs carry the report. The reader can see the shape of the matter. The words were always recited. Only the voice level changed, and it changed for a reason that belonged to a particular moment in Makkah.

**WHAT THE LINE DOES AT THE START OF A WORK**

The reports also describe what the line does. Abū Hurayrah is recorded by ʿAbd al-Qādir al-Ruhāwī in his Forty Hadith collection (al-Arbaʿūn), in a chain that is graded good, that the Prophet ﷺ said every matter of weight that is not begun with the Name of Allah is cut off from blessing. A report from Jābir ibn ʿAbdillāh, and it is weak, paints the day the line came down: the clouds withdrew to the east, the winds settled, the sea rose, and the animals turned their ears to listen. Weak or not, those images carry the feeling the early community had about these four words. They treated the Name as something with weight in it, not a formality to get past before the real words begin.

Think of a man who must cross a wide river. He can step into the boat and trust his own arms, or he can begin by naming the One who made the water, the wood and the strength in his own shoulders. The basmalah is that moment of turning before the first stroke.

**THE MERCY THE LINE NAMES FIRST**

The second half of the line names God twice by one attribute, and the phrase the chapter repeats here, ***“the Most Compassionate, Most Merciful”***, opens the Book on that note rather than on any other. Al-Mukhtaṣar explains that both names describe mercy, and that together they tell the reader how wide it is: it surrounds everything and reaches every living being, and the believers receive the largest share of it. Al-Saʿdī puts it in the old form: the mercy of Allah covers every creature, and it is completed for the people who follow the messengers He sent.

The order carries a lesson. The line does not open with the Mighty, the Judge or the Avenger. It opens with mercy, and it opens with mercy twice. Al-Qurṭubī notes that the Qur'an keeps fear and hope together on purpose. A servant who knows how great Allah is may despair; a servant who hears only about mercy may grow careless. The basmalah teaches both from the first breath: the One you are standing before is great, and the One you are standing before is kind. Al-Qurṭubī brings two Qur'anic lines to prove the pairing: (15:49 — **“Inform My servants ˹O Prophet˺ that I am truly the All-Forgiving, Most Merciful”**), and the line after it, (15:50 — **“and that My torment is indeed the most painful”**). He supports the point with a report in Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim from Abū Hurayrah: if a believer knew the full extent of Allah's punishment, nobody would hope for Paradise, and if an unbeliever knew the full extent of His mercy, nobody would despair of it. Al-Saʿdī adds a point of belief. These are not decorative titles. They tell us that mercy is a real attribute of Allah, and that everything good in the world flows from it, the way light flows from the sun.
verses.2:
> All praise is for Allah—Lord of all worlds

**EVERY KIND OF PRAISE, HANDED TO ONE OWNER**

Ibn Jarīr al-Ṭabarī explains the sentence ***“All praise is for Allah”*** as a declaration that every kind of thanks belongs to Allah alone. It does not belong to any idol, and it does not belong to any creature. He then lists some of the favours behind the thanks: the body that carries out the commands of Allah, the food that keeps the body alive, the guidance that shows a person where to walk. The favours cannot be counted, and the ability to thank Him is itself one of them. He adds a point from the wording. The sentence teaches the servant what to say, as if Allah had said: say that all praise is due to Allah. The first worshipper to use these words was taught them by God.

**PRAISE IS A WIDER WORD THAN THANKS**

The scholars drew a careful line between two words that English uses loosely. Ḥamd is praise given for a quality that deserves it, whether or not the one praising has received anything. Shukr is thanks given for a favour received. Praise is wider because it reaches God's perfection itself, and thanks is narrower because it follows a gift. Al-Rāghib al-Iṣfahānī, quoted in Maʿārif al-Qurʾān, puts it in the plainest form: praise is a wider word than thanks, and the two overlap. This verse opens with praise, and that is why the scholars said the servant here is not merely paying for a favour. He is acknowledging what God is.

**WHAT THE FIRST GENERATION SAID ABOUT THE WORDS**

Ibn Kathīr preserves a report from ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb. He once asked ʿAlī about this phrase. The community already knew what "there is no god but Allah" meant, and "glory be to Allah", and "Allah is greatest"; what did al-ḥamdu lillāh add? ʿAlī answered that it is a statement Allah loved for Himself and was pleased with for Himself, and that He likes to hear it repeated. Ibn ʿAbbās, in a report recorded by Ibn Abī Ḥātim, said that when the servant says these words, Allah answers, "My servant has praised Me."

The definite article carries weight. Ibn Kathīr explains that the al at the front of al-ḥamd gathers every kind of praise. The sentence does not claim one thank-you for Allah. It hands Him all of them. A reader who notices that will see why the chapter does not begin with a request. It begins with a settled account of who is being addressed.

**THE LORD WHO OWNS AND RAISES**

Rabb means owner and master, the one with full authority over what he holds. It also carries a second sense, the one who raises a thing step by step until it reaches its purpose. Maʿārif al-Qurʾān notes that the word belongs to Allah alone, and that a person can only use it for someone else with a qualifier attached, as in "the master of the house".

Al-ʿālamīn, the second half of the verse, is the plural of ʿālam, and it means everything other than Allah. Ibn Kathīr collects the opinions of the early scholars on how wide that is. Al-Farrāʾ and Abū ʿUbayd limited it to beings with minds: the jinn, humankind, the angels and the devils, not the animals. Zayd ibn Aslam and Abū Muḥaysin included everything created with a soul. Qatādah said that every kind of creature is an ʿālam. Al-Qurṭubī concluded that the word covers everything Allah created in this world and the next. The words ***“Lord of all worlds”*** are short, and they place the one who recites them inside a creation too large to count.

The Qur'an shows what this lordship means in practice. When Pharaoh asked Moses who this Lord of all worlds was, the answer was plain: (26:24 — **“˹He is˺ the Lord of the heavens and the earth and everything in between, if only you had sure faith.”**). The chapter's own words return in another place, in a verse that places a person's whole life under that one Owner: (6:162 — **“Say, ‘Surely my prayer, my worship, my life, and my death are all for Allah—Lord of all worlds”**).

**ONE SPRING BEHIND EVERY STREAM**

Maudūdī, in Tazkir al-Qurʾān, draws out why the praise belongs to one Owner. Think of a garden with many streams. Every stream looks separate, and each one waters its own bed. Follow them all back, and the water comes from a single spring. Praise works the same way. When a person admires a flower, a poem, a cure or a kindness, he is admiring something made. Trace it back and it ends at the One who made it.

One habit of the old Arabs shows what the title changed. They spoke of a master of a house, a master of a herd, a master of a caravan. Each one ruled a circle, and the circles did not answer to each other. The verse closes every circle into one. The owner of the house, the herd and the caravan is a single Lord, and the far-off stars belong to Him as surely as the grass underfoot.
verses.3:
> the Most Compassionate, Most Merciful

**TWO NAMES, ONE ROOT, TWO SHAPES**

This verse carries the two names on their own, and it uses exactly the words of the basmalah: ***“the Most Compassionate, Most Merciful”***. The scholars said the repetition is not decoration. The first name states a fact about God, and the second turns that fact toward the people who depend on it.

The two names differ in shape, and the difference is worth knowing. Al-Kashshāf and al-Baḥr al-Muḥīṭ both explain that al-Raḥmān follows the pattern faʿlān, like ghaḍbān for a man filled with anger, while al-Raḥīm follows faʿīl, like raḥīm for someone who shows mercy. The first pattern carries more force, so the scholars said al-Raḥmān holds a fullness that al-Raḥīm does not. Al-Baḥr adds a rule that a reader can test: al-Raḥmān is a description never used for anyone except Allah, just as His Name is not given to anyone else. Al-Bayḍāwī draws the same conclusion from the grammar, noting that the word takes no feminine form, unlike ordinary descriptions, because it belongs to God alone and to no creature.

**A NAME THE MECCANS HAD NEVER HEARD**

The Qur'an shows how the name landed on ears that had never heard it. The polytheists of Makkah were confused by it, and the Qur'an records their question: (25:60 — *“When it is said to them, ‘Prostrate to the Most Compassionate,’ they ask ˹in disgust˺, ‘What is “the Most Compassionate”? Will we prostrate to whatever you order us to?’ And it only drives them farther away”*). The same sūrah that reports the confusion also settles it. Allah told His Prophet ﷺ that either Name may be used in prayer: (17:110 — **“Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ ‘Call upon Allah or call upon the Most Compassionate—whichever you call, He has the Most Beautiful Names.’”**). And the Qur'an states the fact behind both: (20:8 — **“Allah—there is no god ˹worthy of worship˺ except Him. He has the Most Beautiful Names”**).

**HOW WIDE THE MERCY RUNS, AND HOW LONG**

Al-Mukhtaṣar explains that the name al-Raḥmān describes a mercy that surrounds the whole of creation and embraces every living thing. Al-Saʿdī says the same in the language of the early scholars: the mercy of Allah is wide enough to cover every creature He made. The Qur'an states the breadth in one short line: (7:156 — **“But My mercy encompasses everything”**).

Then the second name does a further piece of work. Al-Raḥīm describes the mercy that stays with a person and carries him to the end. Al-Saʿdī draws out the point that protects belief: these two names are not slogans. They tell us that Allah has a real attribute of mercy, that every blessing in the world is a trace of it, and that a hardened heart is not caused by any shortage on His side. The Qur'an gives the same assurance to anyone who has wandered far: (39:53 — **“O My servants who have exceeded the limits against their souls! Do not lose hope in Allah’s mercy, for Allah certainly forgives all sins.”**). Muḥammad Shafīʿ, writing in Maʿārif al-Qurʾān, notices that the name is often joined to the mention of the Hereafter for this reason: it is the mercy that keeps a believer walking until he arrives.

Al-Suyūṭī also records a prayer the Prophet ﷺ taught, which names God as the Merciful of this world and the next: "O You who relieve the anxious, who lift the sorrow, who answer the call of the desperate, the Most Compassionate of this world and the next and their Most Merciful." The chain of that report is weak, and al-Suyūṭī says so. The words themselves show how the community understood the two names. Mercy is not a single act at the end of the road. It runs through this life and the one that follows.

Imagine standing in the rain. The rain falls on the field of the farmer who prepared his soil, and it falls on the rock beside the road, on the good man's roof and on the thief's. That is how the mercy of al-Raḥmān arrives. Now picture the same rain soaked into the fields and turned into a harvest. That is al-Raḥīm: mercy that reaches its purpose in the life of a believer.
verses.4:
> Master of the Day of Judgment

**THE QUESTION THE FOURTH VERSE ANSWERS**

This verse answers the question a reader should be asking by the fourth line. If Allah is Lord of all worlds, what does that lordship mean for me? The answer is a day on which every account is closed, and the verse gives it in five words: ***“Master of the Day of Judgment”***. Al-Qurṭubī notes how the verse follows mercy with mastery, so that hope is never handed a licence to ignore the reckoning. The Book praises mercy twice, and then it names the Owner of the Day the accounts are settled.

**MĀLIK AND MALIK: THE READINGS BEHIND THE WORD**

The first word of the verse was recited in more than one way, and the variations are recorded in detail. Al-Baḥr al-Muḥīṭ lists them. Mālik, on the pattern of fāʿil, was read by ʿĀṣim, al-Kisāʾī, Khalaf in his choice, and Yaʿqūb, and it was the reading of many Companions, among them Ubayy ibn Kaʿb, Ibn Masʿūd, Muʿādh and Ibn ʿAbbās. Malik, on the pattern of faʿīl, was read by the rest of the seven reciters and by other Companions such as Zayd ibn Thābit, Abū al-Dardāʾ and Ibn ʿUmar. Malk and milk, with a stilled or reduced middle, were also heard. The differences do not fight each other. An owner disposes of what he owns as he wishes. A king commands and forbids those under him, and gives out rewards and punishments. The verse names the Day on which both belong to one Lord without a partner.

**WHY THAT ONE DAY IS SINGLED OUT**

Allah is Master of every day. Why single out this one? Al-Saʿdī gives the answer in a picture. On that Day the ownership of every creature breaks and disappears. Kings and ordinary people, owners and those owned, all stand on the same level, all submitted to His greatness, all waiting for His account, hoping for His reward and fearing His punishment. A court where rank survives is not a court; that Day is a court where it does not. Ibn Kathīr answers the same question from another side: on that Day no one claims anything, and no one speaks without permission. Al-Ḍaḥḥāk reports from Ibn ʿAbbās the plain meaning of the verse: on that Day nobody owns what he used to own in the world.

The Qur'an paints that silence more than once. On that Day the spirit and the angels will stand in ranks and none will talk except the one whom the Most Compassionate allows: (78:38 — **“on the Day the ˹holy˺ spirit and the angels will stand in ranks. None will talk, except those granted permission by the Most Compassionate”**). The Qur'an records the hush in one line: (20:108 — **“All voices will be hushed before the Most Compassionate”**). It puts the whole matter into a single announcement: (40:16 — **“Who does all authority belong to this Day? To Allah—the One, the Supreme”**). The two Ṣaḥīḥs record the Prophet ﷺ describing the scene that goes with it. Allah will grasp the earth, fold the heavens in His right hand and call out, "I am the King. Where are the kings of the earth? Where are the tyrants? Where are the arrogant?"

**WHAT THE WORD DĪN CARRIES HERE**

Dīn here means the settling of accounts. Ibn Kathīr supports the meaning from the Qur'an's own use of the word, where it describes a full payment of what is due: (24:25 — **“On that Day, Allah will give them their just penalty in full”**). Maʿārif al-Qurʾān adds a second argument, from fairness. The world is the field of action, not the hall of payment. A rich man may be far from God, and a sick man may be close to Him. If no account were ever settled, the courtroom of justice would stand empty. The Qur'an asks the question twice to wake the reader up: (82:17 — **“What will make you realize what Judgment Day is”**), and then again at (82:18 — **“Again, what will make you realize what Judgment Day is”**).

ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb, in a saying Ibn Kathīr records, left the community a rule for daily life: hold yourselves accountable before you are held accountable, and weigh your deeds before they are weighed. The two Ṣaḥīḥs also record a warning about titles: the most despised name before Allah belongs to a man who calls himself king of kings, because no owner exists except Allah.

Think of a marketplace. All year the traders buy and sell, and nobody is stopped at the gate. Then one morning the gates close for the final audit. Every account book is opened in order, and every deal is read aloud. The verse tells the reader that such a morning is coming, and that the Master of that market is the One being addressed here.
verses.5:
> You ˹alone˺ we worship and You ˹alone˺ we ask for help

**THE TURN FROM SPEAKING ABOUT GOD TO SPEAKING TO HIM**

Until this verse the chapter speaks about God. Here it begins to speak to Him, and the change is the first thing a careful reader notices. Al-Qurṭubī describes what the turn does: the worshipper moves from praise into intimate address in a single step. Al-Bayḍāwī reads the same movement as a walk from proof to sight, so that what the servant knew about his Lord he now says to His face. The classical commentators draw one practical lesson from it. No priest stands between the worshipper and God. Every believer is invited to speak this line himself.

**WHY THE OBJECT OF THE VERB COMES FIRST**

Arabic allows a sentence to be built in more than one order, and this verse puts the object first: ***“You ˹alone˺ we worship”***. Al-Zamakhsharī explains the placement as a device of exclusivity, so that the meaning is that worship is for You alone and for nobody else. Al-Saʿdī states the rule the grammarians use. Fronting the object gives restriction, which is to say the ruling is fixed for the one named and denied to everyone else. Al-Qurṭubī records how naturally the Arabs used that order. A man insulted another and the second man turned away. The first said, "You are the one I mean." The second answered, "And it is you I turn away from."

Al-Baḥr al-Muḥīṭ takes the word iyyāka apart, and its point is modest but useful. The word is a detached pronoun in the accusative case, carrying the meaning "you" as the object of the verb, and it is written with the same shape whether it stands alone or takes a suffix. He also lists the ways the word was recited in different regions: with a heavier or lighter pronunciation of the consonants, with the vowel changed, and in some readings with a light "h" in place of the glottal stop. Al-Baḥr does not treat these as errors to be corrected. He records them as the ordinary variety of a language spread across a continent.

**WHAT THE WORD WORSHIP CARRIES AT ITS ROOT**

Worship here is more than ritual. Al-Ṭabarī reports that the community agreed that the root of the word lies in humility and submission. The same root describes a path that feet have trodden until it is smooth, which is why the word serves both for a road and for a servant. The confession "You alone we worship" therefore says three things at once. You are my Owner, I am Your servant, and I obey You. A person who takes the words seriously cannot say them while following his own opinion in the same breath.

The verse is spoken in the plural, and that is deliberate. The one praying does not stand alone with his private devotion. He speaks as a member of a body that says these words at the same hour across the world, in the same order, facing the same direction. The scholars of the chapter treat that plural as a quiet warning about community. Worship is personal, and it is never private in the sense of belonging to one person only.

**WORSHIP IS SAID BEFORE HELP IS ASKED FOR**

The second half of the verse asks for help, and the order of the two halves is deliberate. A man does not ask a king for help before he has greeted the king and accepted him as king. Picture a worker who walks into a large workshop on his first morning. Before he asks the foreman for tools, he puts himself under the foreman's orders and learns the rules of the house. Only then does he ask, and the tools come.

Al-Ṭabarī defines the request, ***“and You ˹alone˺ we ask for help”***, as the servant asking his Lord for help in worshipping Him, in obeying Him, and in every matter of his life, from no one besides Him. He records a report from Ibn ʿAbbās with exactly that sense, and he is honest about the chain: he grades it weak, and says so. He also draws out the tense of the request. The servant does not ask for help with deeds already finished. He asks for help with what remains of his life, for the strength to do tomorrow what he did not do today.

The Qur'an explains why this help is needed every hour of the day: (47:38 — **“For Allah is the Self-Sufficient, whereas you stand in need ˹of Him˺”**). It names the two tools that carry a person through: (2:45 — **“And seek help through patience and prayer. Indeed, it is a burden except for the humble”**). And it gives the reason the request is answered at all: (40:60 — **“Call upon Me, I will respond to you”**). A servant who keeps these three lines together will not treat supplication as a last resort. It is the ordinary road.

Muslim records the ḥadīth qudsī in which this verse is the hinge of the chapter. Allah says that the prayer is divided between Him and His servant, and that when the servant reaches these words, He answers, "This is between Me and My servant, and My servant shall have what he asks for." Everything before this verse was the servant's praise. Everything after it is his petition.
verses.6:
> Guide us along the Straight Path

**A REQUEST FOR STEADINESS, NOT FOR INFORMATION**

Al-Ṭabarī explains this request in the language of outcome rather than of information. In his reading the verse asks God for success in staying firm on the road: grant us the ability to hold the course, keep us steady in obedience, and set our feet right in what is still ahead of us. He reports from Ibn ʿAbbās, through a chain that runs al-Ḍaḥḥāk's way, the story that Jibrīl told the Prophet ﷺ to say these words, and he takes the explanation from it: the request is for guidance to be placed in the heart. He also notices something worth holding. The request of this verse answers the request of the verse before it. The servant asked for help, and here he says what kind of help he means.

**WHAT GUIDANCE MEANS, AND ITS DEGREES**

Al-Rāghib al-Iṣfahānī, quoted at length in Maʿārif al-Qurʾān, defines guidance as leading someone toward his destination gently and kindly, and he notes that in its fullest sense guidance comes from Allah alone. He describes it in degrees. The first degree is shared by everything created, because every creature was given its nature and then directed to what that nature needs. The Qur'an says it plainly: (20:50 — **“Our Lord is the One Who has given everything its ˹distinctive˺ form, then guided ˹it˺”**). The guidance asked for in this verse is a higher kind: the leading of a person who can choose, toward what pleases God.

The request raises an obvious question. The one praying already believes. Why ask for guidance again, every day, in every prayer? Ibn Kathīr gives the answer that the servant needs his Lord every hour, both to stay firm and to move forward. The Qur'an commands believers to believe, a command that only makes sense as a call to steadiness: (4:136 — **“O believers! Have faith in Allah, His Messenger, the Book He has revealed to His Messenger, and the Scriptures He revealed before”**). It also teaches the prayer that protects what has already been given: (3:8 — **“Our Lord! Do not let our hearts deviate after you have guided us”**).

There is a second question inside the request. God has already shown every human being two roads: (90:10 — **“and shown them the two ways ˹of right and wrong˺”**). Knowing the road exists is not the same as walking it. Maʿārif al-Qurʾān compares guidance to the work of a guide in strange country. A traveller may hold a map, and still need someone who knows the land to walk beside him. The verse is the traveller asking for the companion.

**THE ROAD THAT HAS NO BRANCHES**

Al-Ṭabarī reports that the community agreed on the meaning of the phrase ***“Guide us along the Straight Path”***: it is a clear road with no branches. He supports it with a line of poetry from Jarīr ibn ʿAṭiyyah, who described a leader standing on a road that stays straight while other roads bend. He then notes how the Arabs used the same picture for conduct, calling an honest man straight and a dishonest man crooked, and he concludes that the road the Qur'an names is Islam. The word for straight comes from the same root as standing. A straight road is one that does not lean, and a person who walks it is asked for the same quality.

Ibn Kathīr records the prophetic picture of that road. Aḥmad records in his Musnad the report of an-Nawwās ibn Samʿān, that the Prophet ﷺ described a straight path with two walls on either side, doors standing open in the walls, and curtains hanging over the doors. A caller at the mouth of the path called out, "O people, enter the path and keep straight." Another caller above the path warned anyone reaching for a door, "Do not open it, for if you open it you will pass through." The Prophet ﷺ then named every part of the picture. The path is Islam. The two walls are the limits Allah set. The open doors are what He has forbidden. The caller at the path is the Book of Allah, and the caller above it is the warning Allah places in the heart of every Muslim.

The Qur'an describes the same road from the other end, asking which of two travellers is better off: (67:22 — **“Who is ˹rightly˺ guided: the one who crawls facedown or the one who walks upright on the Straight Path”**). And it gives the road a name that a reader can carry: (6:153 — **“Indeed, that is My Path—perfectly straight. So follow it and do not follow other ways, for they will lead you away from His Way.”**).

A driver who has lost his way in a strange city knows the feeling this verse names. He may have a map on the seat beside him, and every street corner still looks the same in the dark. What he wants is not more information. He wants someone who knows the city to sit beside him and say, turn here. That is the shape of the prayer.
verses.7:
> the Path of those You have blessed—not those You are displeased with, or those who are astray

**THE ROAD IS NAMED BY THE PEOPLE WHO WALK IT**

The verse before this one asked for a road. This verse names the road by the people who walk it, in the words ***“the Path of those You have blessed”***. The Qur'an gives the roster in one line: (4:69 — **“And whoever obeys Allah and the Messenger will be in the company of those blessed by Allah: the prophets, the people of truth, the martyrs, and the righteous—what honourable company”**). Four ranks, one shared description. Every one of them received favour from God, and none of them earned it by right.

Al-Ṭabarī collects the early attempts to identify these people. Ibn ʿAbbās listed the angels, the prophets, the truthful, the martyrs and the righteous, in a report whose chain al-Ṭabarī himself grades weak; the same Ibn ʿAbbās is also recorded as saying simply, the believers. Rabīʿ ibn Anas said they are the prophets. Wakīʿ said the believers, and Ibn Jurayj heard it from Ibn ʿAbbās that way as well. Ibn Zayd read the phrase as the Prophet ﷺ and those with him. Al-Ṭabarī prefers the wider reading, and his reason comes from the text itself. The verse describes people whom God has favoured, and the favour is not limited to one rank. Anyone whom God has favoured, in any generation, is walking on this road.

Al-Zamakhsharī and al-Bayḍāwī both stop at the grammar, and their point is worth having. The phrase "the path of those You have blessed" stands in apposition to "the Straight Path", which means the verse does not just add a description. It defines the road. The straight path is, by God's own naming, the road the blessed ones walked. That gives a reader a way to test any claim to be on the right road: look at where the footprints lead.

**A REPETITION THE EARLY RECITERS KEPT**

The early reciters kept a variant here that is worth knowing. ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb is recorded by Wakīʿ, Abū ʿUbayd and Ibn Abī Dāwūd, along with ʿAbd Allāh ibn al-Zubayr and the Successors ʿIkrimah and al-Aswad, as reciting the line as ghayr al-maghḍūb ʿalayhim wa ghayr al-ḍāllīn, repeating the word "not" before the second group. The meaning does not move: both groups are excluded from the road. The variation shows how carefully the first generation held the words, down to a repeated preposition.

**THOSE WHO KNEW AND TURNED AWAY**

The first failure the verse excludes is the failure of a person who knew the truth and turned away from it. The words are ***“not those You are displeased with”***, and al-Jalālayn and al-Mukhtaṣar both read the phrase that way, with al-Mukhtaṣar tying it to the Israelites, who had the covenant in front of them and did not carry it. The classical identification behind the phrase is the Jews, and the Prophet ﷺ himself gave that answer when he was asked. ʿAbdullāh ibn Shaqīq al-ʿUqaylī reports that the Prophet ﷺ was at Wādī al-Qurā when a man asked him who the people of wrath were, and he answered: the Jews. Ibn Mardawayh records Abū Dharr asking the same question and receiving the same answer. Ibn Kathīr keeps the picture honest, though. Both descriptions, he says, apply to both communities, and he cites the Qur'an for each emphasis: (5:60 — **“It is those who earned Allah’s condemnation and displeasure”**) describes people who were cursed and made targets of wrath, while (5:77 — **“nor follow the vain desires of those who went astray before ˹you˺”**) describes people who wandered and led others to wander.

**THOSE WHO WANDERED WITHOUT LOOKING**

The second failure is softer and more common. The verse closes with the words ***“or those who are astray”***, and al-Mukhtaṣar describes that failure as the condition of a person who did not seek the truth in the first place, tying the description to the Christians, whose mistake lay in the search rather than in the knowledge. The Qur'an uses the word "astray" for exactly this condition, and Ibn Kathīr gathers the places. A person can wander with good intentions and still be far from the road: (4:136 — **“whoever denies Allah, His angels, His Books, His messengers, and the Last Day has clearly gone far astray”**).

ʿAdī ibn Ḥātim heard both answers from the Prophet ﷺ in one sitting, and the report is carried by Aḥmad, by al-Ṭabarī, by Ibn Ḥibbān, and by At-Tirmidhī, who graded it ḥasan. ʿAdī had been a Christian before he accepted Islam, and he came to the Prophet ﷺ with questions. The Prophet ﷺ told him that the people of wrath are the Jews and that the astray are the Christians. ʿAdī's own background gives the report its weight. He was not repeating gossip about strangers. He was being told the truth about the road he had just left and the road he had arrived on.

Two failures, then, and two ways of missing the same road. One traveller studies the timetable, memorises the route, and refuses to board the train. The other never looks at the timetable at all and wanders the platform. A third option is offered by the verse itself: walk with the blessed ones, and let their company be the proof that the road is real.

**ĀMĪN: THE SEAL THE CHAPTER ENDS ON**

The chapter closes with a word that asks God to make all of this true. Muslim records that when the servant recites these last verses, Allah answers, "This is for My servant, and My servant shall have what he asks for." Ibn Kathīr explains the closing Āmīn as the servant's request that his prayer be accepted, and At-Tirmidhī glossed it as a plea not to be let down in hope.

Ibn Kathīr collects the evidence for saying it. Aḥmad, Abū Dāwūd and At-Tirmidhī record Wāʾil ibn Ḥujr hearing the Prophet ﷺ recite the end of the chapter and then say Āmīn, lengthening his voice, and At-Tirmidhī graded the report ḥasan. Abū Mūsā al-Ashʿarī is recorded in Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim being told that when the imam says it, the people behind him should say it too, and God will answer them. A Companion named Abū Zuhayr an-Numayrī, in a report Abū Dāwūd carries with a good chain, used to tell people to seal their prayers with Āmīn, because Āmīn is like a stamp pressed on a page. And ʿĀʾishah, in a report Ibn Mājah records, said that the Jews envied this community for nothing as much as they envied it for Āmīn. The two Ṣaḥīḥs add the promise that sits over the whole chapter: whoever's Āmīn falls together with the Āmīn of the angels has his past sins forgiven.
